hints: Resolve forces vertically: the upward normal reaction $R$ balances the weight $mg$ and the downward component $T\sin 30^\circ$.
Resolve forces horizontally: the pulling component $T\cos 30^\circ$ is balanced by friction $F$.
For the greatest value of $T$ at rest, friction reaches its limiting value $F = \mu R = 0.8R$.
Substitute $R = 0.1(10) + T\sin 30^\circ$ into $T\cos 30^\circ = 0.8R$ and solve for $T$.
walkthrough:
Resolve forces vertically in equilibrium with mass $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$R = mg + T\sin 30^\circ = 0.1(10) + T\sin 30^\circ = 1 + 0.5T$$

Resolve forces horizontally along the rod:
$$F = T\cos 30^\circ$$

Apply the condition for limiting equilibrium $F = \mu R$ with $\mu = 0.8$:
$$T\cos 30^\circ = 0.8(1 + 0.5T)$$
$$T\cos 30^\circ = 0.8 + 0.4T$$

ai_rubric.Using Limiting Equilibrium: Resolves to $R = T\sin 30^\circ + 0.1g$ and equates $T\cos 30^\circ = 0.8R$ to obtain $T = 1.72\text{ N}$.

teacher_walkthrough: Identify the forces acting on the ring. In the vertical direction, the rod exerts an upward normal reaction $R$. Acting downwards are the ring's weight $W = mg = 0.1(10) = 1\text{ N}$ and the vertical component of the applied force $T\sin 30^\circ$.

State the vertical equilibrium condition:
$$\sum F_y = 0$$
$$R - mg - T\sin 30^\circ = 0$$
$$R = 0.1(10) + T\sin 30^\circ = 1 + 0.5T$$

State the horizontal equilibrium condition. The horizontal component of the pulling force is $T\cos 30^\circ$, which is resisted by the friction force $F$:
$$\sum F_x = 0$$
$$F = T\cos 30^\circ$$

State the limiting friction law. For the greatest force $T$ where the ring remains at rest, the friction force reaches its maximum possible value:
$$F = \mu R$$
Substitute $\mu = 0.8$, $F = T\cos 30^\circ$, and $R = 1 + 0.5T$:
$$T\cos 30^\circ = 0.8(1 + 0.5T)$$
$$T\cos 30^\circ = 0.8 + 0.4T$$

hints: With $T = 3\text{ N}$, recompute the normal reaction $R = 0.1(10) + 3\sin 30^\circ$.
Because $T > 1.72\text{ N}$, the ring accelerates and friction is limiting: $F = \mu R = 0.8R$.
Apply Newton's second law horizontally: $3\cos 30^\circ - F = ma$, where $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$, and solve for $a$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the normal reaction when $T = 3\text{ N}$:
$$R = 0.1g + 3\sin 30^\circ = 0.1(10) + 3(0.5) = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5\text{ N}$$

Calculate the limiting friction force opposing motion with $\mu = 0.8$:
$$F = \mu R = 0.8(2.5) = 2\text{ N}$$

Apply Newton's second law horizontally with mass $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$:
$$3\cos 30^\circ - F = ma$$
$$3\cos 30^\circ - 2 = 0.1a$$
$$2.598076 - 2 = 0.1a$$
$$0.1a = 0.598076 \implies a = \frac{0.598076}{0.1} \approx 5.98\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

ai_rubric.Applying Newton's Second Law: Calculates $R = 2.5\text{ N}$, forms $3\cos 30^\circ - 0.8(2.5) = 0.1a$, and solves for $a = 5.98\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

teacher_walkthrough:
Determine the normal reaction $R$ perpendicular to the rod when the applied force is $T = 3\text{ N}$:
$$R = mg + T\sin 30^\circ$$
Substitute $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $T = 3\text{ N}$:
$$R = 0.1(10) + 3(0.5) = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5\text{ N}$$

Since the ring accelerates along the rod, the friction force takes its maximum limiting value:
$$F = \mu R = 0.8 \times 2.5 = 2\text{ N}$$

State Newton's second law for motion along the horizontal rod:
$$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$
$$T\cos 30^\circ - F = ma$$
Substitute $T = 3\text{ N}$, $F = 2\text{ N}$, and $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$:
$$3\cos 30^\circ - 2 = 0.1a$$

Evaluate the numerical terms step-by-step:
$$3\cos 30^\circ = 3 \times 0.866025 = 2.598076$$
$$2.598076 - 2 = 0.598076$$
$$0.1a = 0.598076$$
Divide both sides by $0.1$:
$$a = \frac{0.598076}{0.1} \approx 5.98\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
